property_summary: Only the owner can cause the contract C to send its entire balance to an arbitrary recipient (withdrawAll succeeds only when called by the owner).
withdrawAll reverts for callers who are not the owner (i.e., non-owner callers cannot successfully invoke withdrawAll).
If the caller is not equal to C.owner(), then calling withdrawAll must revert (i.e., withdrawAll only succeeds when msg.sender == owner).
For any provided caller address not equal to c.owner(), invoking withdrawAll should revert (i.e., non-owners cannot successfully cause withdrawAll to complete).
If a caller address is not equal to C.owner(), then calling withdrawAll must revert (withdrawAll only succeeds when msg.sender == owner).

For any caller and recipient, only the owner can successfully empty the contract balance via withdrawAll(address); the mutant that removes the owner check allows non-owners to withdraw (so for some caller/recipient inputs the mutant yields a different result).

After owner funds the contract and calls withdrawAll to a recipient, the recipient receives the entire contract balance (so c.balance becomes 0 and recipient balance increases by the full previous contract balance).
If caller is not the owner, withdrawAll must revert (so reverted == true when msg.sender != c.owner()).
When the owner calls withdrawAll, the call must revert if the contract's balance is zero (i.e., owner cannot successfully withdraw when balance is zero).
If the provided ownerCaller equals this test contract and c's balance is zero before the call, then calling c.withdrawAll(recipient) must revert.
If ownerCaller equals this contract and c.balance == 0 before the call, then calling c.withdrawAll(recipient) must revert.
Only the owner can successfully make the contract transfer its entire balance to a recipient (i.e., withdrawAll only succeeds when called by owner).
Only the owner is allowed to successfully call withdrawAll (non-owners must have the call revert).
Only the contract owner can successfully call withdrawAll (calls by non-owners always revert).
If withdrawAll call by msg.sender does not revert then the caller must be the recorded owner (c.owner()).

If withdrawAll call succeeds (does not revert) then msg.sender equals c.owner(), and if msg.sender equals c.owner() then withdrawAll reverts (i.e., exactly owners are allowed and non-owners are forbidden).

For every caller address, the reference contract only allows the owner to successfully transfer the contract balance via withdrawAll (calls by non-owners do not transfer funds / do not change address(c).balance), whereas the mutant inverts the check and allows non-owners to withdraw, so there exist callers that change address(c).balance in the mutant but not in the reference.
After c.withdrawAll is called by the owner sending funds out, the contract balance becomes zero regardless of the recipient address.
When withdrawAll is called by owner it always empties contract C's balance (leaves address(c).balance == 0).
For any caller, withdrawAll never reverts (i.e., always succeeds) when called by the owner.
If withdrawAll is invoked by a non-owner, it reverts; only the owner can successfully call withdrawAll (so reverted == (msg.sender != c.owner())).
When withdrawAll is called by the owner, the call never reverts (succeeds) and the caller's address(this).balance increases by the amount that was drained from C (i.e., owner receives funds).
When a non-owner calls withdrawAll, the call always reverts (only the owner can succeed).

If the recipient reverts when receiving Ether, the reference (using transfer) causes withdrawAll to revert (no Ether leaves the contract), whereas the mutant using call may behave differently by catching/propagating return value semantics causing a different observable outcome; thus for all inputs the reference either reverts or leaves balance unchanged when recipient reverts, but the mutant can succeed and change c.balance for some recipient that reverts on transfer but not on call return value behavior.

For every recipient address that can receive funds via transfer (i.e. its receive() / fallback() does not revert for 2300 gas), calling withdrawAll by the owner always reduces contract balance to zero (all funds forwarded) — the mutant that uses call may leave the contract balance nonzero for some recipient implementations that accept call but cause transfer to revert or vice versa, so a recipient that reverts on transfer but allows call will make the mutant succeed while the reference reverts (and thus balance stays), violating the rule.

For any recipient contract that reverts when given only 2300 gas (so transfer fails), the correct contract's withdrawAll always reverts (leaving address(c).balance unchanged) while the mutant that uses call can succeed for some such recipients — so the invariant is: when a recipient's fallback consumes/reverts under 2300 gas, withdrawAll must revert and preserve c.balance; the mutant breaks this for some recipients.

For any recipient contract whose fallback consumes more than 2300 gas (causing transfer to revert), the reference C's withdrawAll (which uses transfer) will revert and leave address(c).balance unchanged for all inputs, whereas the mutant using call can succeed and drain the balance for some such recipient; the test asserts that withdrawAll called by owner either reverts (ok==false) or leaves contract balance zero — the reference always leaves balance unchanged when recipient intentionally reverts on transfer, but the mutant will sometimes succeed (ok==true and balance==0), violating the invariant.

For any recipient and any amount funded to C, when the owner calls withdrawAll the contract's balance becomes zero (all funds are forwarded); the mutant using call+require can leave the contract balance nonzero for some recipient behaviours (specifically a reentrant attacker that drains partially or causes different gas/flow), so the rule is violated by the mutant for some fuzzed inputs.
After a successful withdrawAll by owner, the target contract remains extant (its balance is 0 but its address still has nonzero code), i.e. address(c).balance == 0 and address(c).code.length > 0.
Calling withdrawAll should not revert when msg.sender is the contract's owner.
When withdrawAll is called by the owner, the call succeeds (does not revert) and the contract remains existent (its code is not selfdestructed).
If the withdrawAll call by the stored owner does not revert, then the contract's code length must be > 0.
If the withdrawAll call did not revert when invoked from the stored owner, then the contract's code must still be present (address(c).code.length > 0).

After any successful withdrawAll(recipient) call by the owner, the contract C remains deployed and retains address(c).balance == 0 (i.e., it is not self-destructed); the mutant that calls selfdestruct breaks this by making the contract destroyed (address(c).balance == 0 still holds but the contract code is removed), so we check that the contract's code size is nonzero by observing a call to a view (the owner getter) — in the reference the call succeeds for all inputs, but in the mutant the call will revert/return empty for some inputs because the contract is destroyed.

After any successful withdrawAll(...) call made by the owner with any recipient and any starting balance, the contract remains callable (its public owner getter still returns the owner); the mutant that self-destructs breaks this because after withdrawal the contract's code is removed and calling the public getter will revert/return empty for some inputs.

For any caller and recipient and any starting balance, if the owner calls withdrawAll sending the contract's entire balance to the recipient, then afterward the contract's owner getter remains callable (call succeeds and returns the original owner); the mutant that selfdestructs can break this because the contract may be destroyed and its getter call will fail.

For any caller address that is the owner and any recipient address and any starting balance, after calling withdrawAll(recipient) the contract remains deployed so that a subsequent zero-value call to the contract (a low-level call) succeeds (returns true); the mutant that selfdestructs can make that subsequent low-level call fail for some inputs (because the contract is destroyed).

For any owner caller and any recipient and starting balance, when the owner calls withdrawAll(recipient) the call to withdrawAll always succeeds (does not revert) on the reference; the mutant that self-destructs can make a subsequent call to the public owner getter revert/return empty, so we instead observe that after owner withdrawAll the contract still responds to a zero-value external call to its owner() getter (i.e. the call succeeds), which the self-destructing mutant can break for some inputs.
